name: Ivan Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be published with your name on it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on rotating shifts at a plastics plant out on the industrial estate, so a normal day might actually be a night. I run two injection moulding presses that make clips and trim pieces for car doors. Mostly I pull parts off the conveyor, check them for flash, that's the thin bit of plastic that leaks out at the seam, and pack them in crates. Marek, the setter, still has to sort it when a mould sticks, because I'm not trusted with that yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. You finish a shift and there's a stack of crates that wasn't there before. What wears me out is the heat off the presses in summer and the nights, because my girlfriend Lena works days at a care home and some weeks we only properly see each other on Sundays. And every few months management brings in some new touchscreen, and I'm always the last one to get the hang of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year someone in the canteen says the robots are coming, and every year we're still here pulling parts. I'd probably put something sarcastic in the union group chat, like 'so much for the future'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. I'm not quick with new stuff, and if nothing big changes I can keep learning the presses at my own speed. Marek says it took him five years to get good at setting, and I'd like my five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep putting a bit away each month, and maybe finally ask Marek to teach me mould changes. Lena and I talked about getting a bigger flat next year, and I'd still go ahead with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, I think. A bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even in this picture, some routine tasks get automated. Which bit of your job would you guess goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checking, probably. Last year they trialled a camera on press four that looks for flash and short shots, and it threw out good parts half the time, so they switched it off. If they got that working, I'd lose the one part of my job where I actually use my eyes, and I'd just be packing crates. That's not a disaster, but it's duller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if that camera came back and worked, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grumble, mainly. I'd ask our union rep, Dawn, whether they can cut a job because of it, and she'd say not without consultation. Then I'd get on with it. I'm not going to fight a camera.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so: every year someone says the robots are coming and we're still here pulling parts. I'd post something sarcastic in the union group chat.
S0.think: It'd be a relief, because I'm slow with new things and this gives me time to learn the presses at my own speed. I'd like the five years Marek had to get good at setting.
S0.do: Carries on with his shifts and keeps saving a little each month. Asks Marek to teach him mould changes and goes ahead with the bigger flat next year. If a quality camera returns, checks with the union rep and then accepts it.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, with mild irritation at the idea of losing the checking part of the job.
S0.quote: Every year someone in the canteen says the robots are coming, and every year we're still here pulling parts.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan's relief is about pace more than about AI itself: he knows he learns slowly and wants time. The failed camera trial on press four is his proof that the hype is overblown. He reaches for the union by reflex, even on small changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: fine, bring in the machines, but the people who built this place get a share and get trained first. I'd be in the group chat telling people to come to meetings. Not that many of them do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm exactly the person they'd let go. I'm junior, I'm slow on the screens, and my job is pulling parts off a belt, which a robot arm already does at the big plant up the road. I don't think I'd be one of the people who adapts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a deal on retraining and no forced redundancies. I'd drop the bigger flat plan and try to get our savings from about three months up to six. If they offered training I'd go, but I wouldn't go looking for courses on my own. I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the stomach. Angry at the owners, mostly, and a bit ashamed that I'm not better at this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Sam. He's been on packing for nineteen years, he doesn't read well, and the touchscreens already make him sweat. If they put a robot arm on his line he's gone, and he's got nowhere to go. Me, at least I'm young. Sam's fifty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to training if it's offered but not look for it yourself. If nobody offers it, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd probably end up at the warehouse on the ring road, or at another plastics plant that hasn't upgraded yet. There are a few around. I know that's just running from it, but running is what I'd do. Lena would push me to do a course, and maybe she'd win.

S1.say: Bring in the machines, but the people who built this place get a share and get trained first. I'd be telling people in the group chat to come to union meetings.
S1.think: I'm exactly the person they'd let go: junior, slow on screens, doing a job a robot arm already does up the road. I don't think I'd be one of the ones who adapts.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting to push for retraining and no forced redundancies. Drops the bigger flat and tries to build savings from about three months to six. If no training is offered, moves to a warehouse or an older plastics plant nearby.
S1.feel: A knot in his stomach, anger at the owners, and some shame about being slow.
S1.quote: I know that's just running from it, but running is what I'd do.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is confident and collective, but privately he expects to be first out. He's honest that he'd move sideways to an older plant rather than retrain. His worry for Big Sam, aged fifty-four, came quickly and seemed to steady him: he sees himself as one of the lucky ones for being young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of tech companies run everything. I'd share every petition going and tell people to strike before it's too late. Somebody has to say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no trade, because the one trade I'm half learning is the one the robots take. And if even Lena's care work goes to robots, we've got nothing. I don't see a way out of that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: takeaways, the car if we could manage without it, the lot, and keep every penny. I'd be on the union's back to fight for a redundancy deal and for a government income for people pushed out. If the plant closed, I'd move back in with my mum and put our names down for whatever support there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's gone. I think I'd be lying awake every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are only two years in this picture. What changes because the warning is that short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, because I'm slow. Give me ten years and maybe I'd drag myself through something. Give me two and I'm still trying to learn how to change a mould when the robot that changes moulds arrives. There's no time for someone like me to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it'll be fine, which is a lie, and she'd see straight through it. Then we'd sit with the bank app open and work out how many months we'd last. The answer would be about three.

S2.say: This is what happens when a handful of tech companies run everything. I'd share every petition and tell people to strike before it's too late.
S2.think: In two years I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no trade, and if Lena's care work goes too we've got nothing. I don't see a way out for me.
S2.do: Cuts all spending at once, including the car if possible, and keeps every penny. Presses the union for a redundancy deal and backs calls for a government income. If the plant closes, moves back in with his mum and signs up for support.
S2.feel: Sick and unmoored, expecting to lie awake every night.
S2.quote: I'm still trying to learn how to change a mould when the robot that changes moulds arrives.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning hits him hardest because he sees himself as a slow learner with no time to catch up. The bank-app moment with Lena, and his flat 'about three' months, was the most raw thing he said. All his options are defensive: cut, fight, fall back on family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but louder: we've got five years, so governments need a plan now, not after. I'd go on the marches. I'd tell everyone at work to join the union while it still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but not by enough for me. I'd be thirty-two. I think I'd use the time to get angry and organised more than to change myself. That's probably a mistake, but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up as a union workplace rep, if Dawn would have me, and spend the first couple of years building numbers. I'd put money aside every month, aiming for a year of bills. Lena and I would keep renting, no mortgage, nothing that ties us down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's something to do with the worry. That helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said using the time to change yourself is a mistake you'd probably make anyway. Why not retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because retrain into what? Every course I could do, the AI does it by 2031 too. My cousin did a coding course three years ago and he's already struggling. At least a union is people standing together, and that doesn't get automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you picture the day it arrives, five years from now, what do you see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The press hall with the lights off. They don't need lights for robots. I'd probably go in for the last shift just to see it, and then go to the pub with Marek and Sam.

S3.say: We've got five years, so governments need a plan now, not afterwards. I'd go on the marches and tell everyone at work to join the union while it still means something.
S3.think: Five years is better but not by enough for me; I'd be thirty-two. I'd use the time to get angry and organised more than to change myself, which is probably a mistake.
S3.do: Volunteers as a union workplace rep and spends two years building membership. Saves every month towards a year of bills. Keeps renting with Lena and avoids a mortgage.
S3.feel: Worried, but steadier because there's something to do with the worry.
S3.quote: The press hall with the lights off. They don't need lights for robots.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time turns his fear into organising rather than retraining. He rejects courses on the grounds that AGI makes every course pointless, citing a struggling cousin. He knows this is partly an excuse and says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say, right, no excuses, this is when we fight for proper rules: taxes on robots, shorter weeks, a share for workers. I'd say it in the canteen and I'd vote on it. Ten years is two elections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to get properly good at my job and then watch it go. I'd be thirty-seven. Part of me thinks I'd just keep my head down and hope it's slower than they say. Things usually are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the plant, keep going with the union, and keep saving steadily, a bit more each year. I probably wouldn't start anything new for the first few years, I'd just wait and see if it's real. Lena would want us to think about kids, and I'd want to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could sleep. Ten years feels like forever when you're twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to wait on kids. Is that because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. I don't want to bring a kid into a house where neither of us has a job in 2036. But I'd also say that if nothing was happening, so maybe it's an excuse. Lena would call it one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd do, compared with the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. I'd do the same things, just slower. The difference is I wouldn't be panicking, so maybe I'd make better choices. Or I'd waste it. I've wasted time before.

S4.say: Ten years is two elections, so this is when we fight for proper rules: taxes on robots, shorter weeks and a share for workers. I'd say it in the canteen and at the ballot box.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to get good at my job and then watch it go. Part of me would keep my head down and hope it's slower than they say.
S4.do: Stays at the plant, stays active in the union and raises his savings a little each year. Holds off on anything new for the first few years to see if it's real. Wants to delay having children with Lena.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to sleep; ten years feels long at twenty-seven.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to get properly good at my job and then watch it go.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning mostly slows him down rather than changing his plan. He admits he might waste the decade, and that 'waiting on kids' may be an excuse he'd use anyway. His politics sharpen here: robot taxes and shorter weeks are concrete asks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is companies having to keep people on and train them while the robots come in, and the government paying people properly when the work goes. Not a scheme where you fill in forms for six months. Just money in the bank while you sort yourself out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole thing, really. If the people who lose the jobs owned a bit of the machines, I wouldn't mind half as much.

headlineQuote: If the people who lose the jobs owned a bit of the machines, I wouldn't mind half as much.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old junior operator on rotating shifts at a plastics plant, running injection moulding presses that make car door clips, and living in a rented flat with his girlfriend Lena, a care worker. He knows he learns slowly, avoids new technology and leans on the union his instincts trust. A plateau would be a relief, steady change would push him into union meetings and a sideways move to an older plant, and fast AGI leaves him panicked, counting about three months of savings. More warning time makes him angrier and more organised, but not much more willing to retrain.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have no time to catch up as a slow learner and no trade to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Companies made to keep and train people while robots come in, and proper government payments without months of forms. He also wants workers to own a share of the machines.
